::: {.lead}
Level 1 of *Rooftop Rescue* has two kinds of moments. In some, the player
**watches**: Salma begs on the roof, and the camera shows her fear. In
others, the player **plays**: Nour rows between floating boxes, and Pasha the
cat jumps from the roof into her net. A storyboard for a film shows only the
first kind. A game needs both, and the second kind must also show what the
player sees on the screen, what the player does, and what the game answers.
In lectures 9 and 10 you drew boards for a cutscene. In this lesson you draw
**gameplay** panels, you time a board as an **animatic**, and you meet the
tools that make storyboards in the lab. Every section ends with a short
task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary storyboard cutscene gameplay-storyboard hud player-input feedback fail-state animatic pacing storyboard-template >}}

## 11.1 Watch or play? Two kinds of boards

The team of *Night Owl Games* lists the moments of level 1. For each one it
asks: does the player watch, or play? The answer decides the board
(@fig-two).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.1 — Cutscene and gameplay storyboards"}
A **cutscene storyboard** plans a moment the player only watches: the team
chooses every shot. A **gameplay storyboard** plans a moment the player
plays: it shows the player's view, the **HUD**, the **player input** and
the game's **feedback**.
:::

![A cutscene panel (the team chooses the close-up) and a gameplay panel (the player's view with the HUD and the input).](images/cut-vs-play.png){#fig-two width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.1 — The moments of level 1"}
1. "Salma begs on the roof." The player watches: a cutscene board with a
   close-up.
2. "Nour rows between floating boxes." The player swipes: a gameplay board.
3. "Pasha jumps; the player taps to catch." The player taps: a gameplay
   board.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.2 — The camera in gameplay"}
In a cutscene, the shot can change in every panel. In gameplay, the camera
usually follows rules (for example, it follows the boat from the side), so
gameplay panels often keep the same view. What changes is the action, the
HUD and the feedback.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing gameplay like a film: a close-up of a face while the player must
steer a boat. The player cannot see the boxes and loses control. In
gameplay, show what the player needs to play.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch or play?"}
Choose a mobile game you know. Write four of its moments.

1. For each moment, write "watch" or "play".
2. For one "play" moment, write what is on the screen: the HUD, and what the
   player does.

*Your result:* four moments with their kind, and one screen described.
:::

## 11.2 What a gameplay panel shows

A gameplay panel must answer four questions: what does the player see, what
does the player do, how does the game answer, and what happens if the player
fails (@fig-gameplay)?

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.2 — The parts of a gameplay panel"}
A gameplay panel shows: the **player's view** (the game camera); the **HUD**
(lives, score, a map) where the game shows it; the **player input** as an
icon (a tap, a swipe, a button); the **feedback** (a sound, a flash, points);
and, in a next panel, the **fail state**: what the game shows when the player
does not succeed.
:::

![A gameplay board: the swipe, then success (+100) and fail (splash, one heart lost).](images/gameplay-board.png){#fig-gameplay width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.3 — The rowing board"}
1. Panel 1: the boat from the side; the HUD (three hearts, the score); a
   swipe icon; an arrow to the right.
2. Panel 2a (success): the boat passes the box; "+100" pops up.
3. Panel 2b (fail): the boat hits the box; a splash; one heart grey; the
   caption says "try again from panel 1".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.4 — Feedback in the caption"}
Some feedback cannot be drawn. The caption says it: "SFX: splash. The phone
vibrates. The heart shakes and turns grey."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing only the success. Players fail often, and the fail state is part of
the experience: what they see, hear and do next must be planned too.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · One gameplay moment"}
Take the "play" moment of your game from section 11.1.

1. Draw two panels: the player's action, and the success.
2. Draw a third panel for the fail state. Add the HUD and an input icon.

*Your result:* three gameplay panels with captions.
:::

## 11.3 Is the timing right? The animatic

A board on paper does not show time. The team wants to feel the **pacing**:
does a line stay long enough to read? Does a shot drag? It makes an
**animatic** (@fig-animatic).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.3 — Animatic"}
An **animatic** plays the panels of a storyboard one after the other, each
for its planned time, with simple sound (lines, effects). It is the first
"video" of a scene, made before any 3D work.
:::

![The six panels of the opening on a time line: 16 s in total.](images/animatic.png){#fig-animatic width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.5 — Timing the opening"}
The six panels of the opening have 3, 3, 2, 3, 2 and 2 seconds.

1. Total: 15 s; the producer wants 12 to 16 s.
2. In the animatic, Salma's line (2 s) is gone before the player has read
   it. The team gives it 3 s.
3. New total: 16 s, still inside the limit.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Timing panels by the drawing, not by the content. A line of dialogue needs
the time to read it; an action needs the time to happen.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/animatic-player.html" poster="sims/animatic-player.png" title="Animatic Player: time the opening" height="740" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Time the opening"}
Open **Animatic Player** (above, or scan the QR code).

1. Press Play and watch the six panels. Which panel feels too short?
2. Change the times so that the check passes. Write your six times.

*Your result:* six times, the total and one sentence about the pacing.
:::

## 11.4 Tools: from paper to an animatic

Storyboards do not need expensive software. The lab has enough
(@fig-tools).

| Tool | Good for |
|---|---|
| Paper and a storyboard template | fast thumbnails; works without a computer |
| PowerPoint (or Google Slides) | one slide per panel, the caption in the notes; slide timings and File › Export › Create a Video make an animatic |
| A free drawing app (Krita) | clean panels with layers |
| A free storyboard app (Storyboarder) | panels, captions and timing in one place |

: Storyboard tools. {#tbl-tools}

![Four ways to make a storyboard in the lab.](images/board-tools.png){#fig-tools width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.6 — An animatic in PowerPoint"}
1. Insert one picture (photo of a panel) per slide; type the caption in the
   speaker notes.
2. Transitions › After: set each slide's time (3 s, 3 s, 2 s, …).
3. Insert › Audio adds the sound; File › Export › Create a Video gives an MP4
   animatic.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Spending the time on the tool, not on the board. Start on paper; move to a
tool only to time, clean and share the board.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Three slides, one animatic"}
Take a photo of three of your panels with your phone.

1. In PowerPoint, put one photo per slide and the caption in the notes.
2. Set the times (Transitions › After) and play the slide show.

*Your result:* a file `animatic.pptx` with three timed slides.
:::

## Case study: Cut or Play? Planning level 1

*Night Owl Games* plans the boards of level 1 of *Rooftop Rescue*. The team
must decide which moments are cutscenes (Salma begs on the roof) and which
are gameplay (Nour rows between boxes by swiping; Pasha jumps and the player
taps to catch). For the gameplay boards it must show the swipe, the HUD and
the fail state (a splash and one heart lost), and it wants a quick animatic
made in the lab. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
decisions. In the mini-game below you plan them.

{{< sim file="sims/cut-or-play.html" poster="sims/cut-or-play.png" title="Cut or Play? Plan the boards of level 1" kind="game" height="760" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on interface and
feedback (what the player needs to see) and on story and gameplay. Microsoft
Support, "Turn your presentation into a video".

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between a cutscene board and a gameplay board?
2. Name four things that a gameplay panel shows.
3. Why does a gameplay panel often keep the same view?
4. What is a fail state? Give an example from *Rooftop Rescue*.
5. How do you show feedback that cannot be drawn, such as a vibration?
6. What is an animatic? What does it show that paper does not?
7. Six panels have 2, 3, 3, 2, 3 and 2 s. What is the total?
8. A line of dialogue is on screen for 1 s. What is the problem?
9. Name two free or lab tools for storyboards.
10. How do you make an animatic in PowerPoint?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A cutscene board plans a moment the player watches; a gameplay board a moment the player plays, with the player's view, HUD, input and feedback.
2. The player's view, the HUD, the player input, the feedback (and the fail state).
3. In gameplay the camera follows rules (for example it follows the boat); the action changes.
4. What the game shows when the player does not succeed: a splash and one heart lost.
5. In the caption: "The phone vibrates."
6. The panels played with their times and sound; it shows the pacing.
7. 15 s.
8. The player cannot read it in time.
9. For example paper with a template, PowerPoint, Krita, Storyboarder.
10. One slide per panel, timings in Transitions › After, then File › Export › Create a Video.
:::
